findings.title: DeleteCollection records storage metric for legacy call
findings.body: In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` is called after `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...)`. It should be `d.recordLegacyDuration` because the call is to LegacyStorage, not Storage. As written, every legacy delete-collection failure will be misattributed to Storage in metrics, defeating monitoring and SLO alerting on the legacy path.

findings.title: Create error path records legacy metric using storage timer
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Two problems: (1) it records a legacy duration even though the legacy was never called; (2) the duration it computes is for Storage (startStorage), not Legacy. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The same bug exists for Update on line 129. Effect: storage failures will be miscounted as legacy failures and the recorded duration will not correspond to the failing call.

findings.title: Update error path records legacy metric using storage timer
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Same issue as the Create error path: this should be `d.recordStorageDuration` because the error happened in Storage, and the timer being measured (`startStorage`) corresponds to Storage, not Legacy. Storage update failures will be misattributed to the legacy path in metrics.

findings.title: Async legacy write derives context from cancelled request context
findings.body: All four async goroutines (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) build their timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` where `ctx` is the request context (`klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` from the outer function). When the originating HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled and the derived context is immediately cancelled as well, so the 10s timeout is effectively zero. The whole point of mode 3 is to mirror writes to legacy as a safety net; with a cancelled parent context this safety net is dropped on every request that returns before the goroutine schedules. The legacy-mirror call should be made independent of request lifetime (e.g., derive from a long-lived background context) so that the write actually completes after the response is sent.

findings.title: Same objInfo reused for Storage and Legacy Update calls
findings.body: `objInfo` is passed to `d.Storage.Update` and then, in the goroutine, to `d.Legacy.Update` unchanged. `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` implementations are commonly stateful (the previous version of this file explicitly wrapped it in `updateWrapper` and supplied a fresh wrapper holding the updated object for the legacy call). Reusing objInfo risks the legacy update either re-fetching the pre-update object, returning stale data, or returning an error from the second `UpdatedObject` invocation. This is a behavioural regression from the prior implementation in this same function.

findings.title: Async legacy goroutines have no panic recovery
findings.body: The four `go func()` blocks (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) call into legacy storage and record metrics without any panic recovery. A panic inside the legacy storage adapter or in the metric call will crash the process because Go panics in unrecovered goroutines are fatal. Each goroutine should at minimum `defer recover()` and log the recovered value so that a single failing legacy backend cannot bring down the API server.

findings.title: Delete records storage metric with name as kind label
findings.body: In Delete, the success-path metric is `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. All other methods use `options.Kind` as the third argument (the resource-kind label). Passing `name` here will produce a different label cardinality and break any dashboard or alert that aggregates by kind for delete operations. It should be `options.Kind` to be consistent with Create/Update/DeleteCollection and with the legacy-error metric on line 113.

findings.title: Delete sets klog context with d.Log instead of enriched log
findings.body: Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection all do `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` using the `log` variable enriched via `WithValues("name", ..., "kind", ..., "method", ...)`. Delete instead does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so any subsequent log line (including the legacy call inside the goroutine) loses the request-scoped "name"/"kind"/"method" values, making debugging harder. It should use the enriched `log` variable.

findings.title: defer cancel() placed after side-effecting line in Update goroutine
findings.body: In the Update goroutine, `defer cancel()` is placed between `startLegacy := time.Now()` and the `d.Legacy.Update` call. While functionally correct (defer runs at function exit), it is stylistically inconsistent with the Create/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines, which put `defer cancel()` immediately after the `context.WithTimeoutCause` call. Easy fix: move the deferred cancel directly under the WithTimeoutCause call.

findings.title: Legacy mirror timeout is a hardcoded magic number
findings.body: `time.Second*10` appears as the timeout for the legacy-mirror context in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. This should be a configurable constant (or a field on DualWriterMode3) so it can be tuned per resource type and tested; otherwise changing it requires editing four call sites.

findings.title: TestMode3_Get uses local prometheus registry instead of shared one
findings.body: Only `TestMode3_Get` creates its own registry with `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()`. Every other TestMode3_* test uses the package-level `p`. The dual-writer change in `dualwriter_mode1_test.go` removed the same leftover in mode1, but the corresponding cleanup was missed in `TestMode3_Get`. Use the shared `p` for consistency and to avoid duplicate registries across tests.

findings.title: Tests do not verify async legacy write actually occurred
findings.body: In TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection the legacy call is dispatched in a goroutine after the request returns, but the test only asserts on the synchronous return value. There is no synchronization (no WaitGroup, channel, or `m.AssertExpectations`) to ensure the legacy mock was actually invoked before the test exits. A regression where the goroutine no longer runs (e.g., refactor that accidentally makes the legacy call synchronous-but-skipped) would pass these tests silently. Add a synchronization mechanism (e.g., a `sync.WaitGroup` toggled in the goroutine, or use a channel signaled by a mock callback) and call `m.AssertExpectations(t)` to assert the legacy side effect actually happened.

findings.title: TestMode3_Create failure case sets up the wrong store's mock
findings.body: The second test case in TestMode3_Create is named "error when creating object in the unified store fails" and expects `wantErr: true`, but the expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` against the legacy store. Because the test wires both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` to the same `mock.Mock{}`, the expectation ends up firing on whichever call runs first (the storage call), so the test happens to pass for the wrong reason. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, this case will silently flip to passing on the legacy path and the error will be swallowed by the async goroutine. Either rename the case or register the expectation against the storage mock explicitly.
